new_statements.quote: While there are a handful of monosyllabic lexical items, most Malagasy roots are di- or trisyllabic. Most words have primary lexical stress on the penultimate syllable. However, lexical items ending in one of the "weak final syllables" (-na, -ka, -tra in Merina; -ke, -tse in western and southwestern dialects (Dahl 1952); -gnV, -kV, -trV in North Betsimisaraka (O'Neill 2015) and Tsimihety (Dahl 1952; Tsimilaza 1981)) have antepenultimate stress, and a small number of words have final-syllable stress. [p.24:] the Southwestern group includes Masikoro Vezo Mahafaly and Tandroy.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level, second-hand for Mahafaly: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root; roots ending in a weak final syllable (in the south-western dialects, to which Mahafaly belongs, -ke, -tse; Adelaar's two Mahafaly forms show -kĕ behaving this way: tùmbukĕ, rànju) carry antepenultimate stress; a small number of roots are final-stressed. Suffixation moves primary stress one syllable to the right.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Howe p.48: 'In longer words, certain syllables prior to the syllable bearing primary stress receive secondary stress'; in compounds primary stress on the rightmost member, secondary on the others (p.49). Stated for Malagasy generally, not for Mahafaly.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak-final roots (-ke, -tse in SW dialects) = antepenultimate; a small number of final-stressed words; stress is lexically contrastive in minimal pairs (Merina examples).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word (root) level, citation forms, with stress shift under suffixation. The statement is pan-Malagasy with an explicit sub-clause for 'western and southwestern dialects' credited to Dahl 1952; Mahafaly is placed in the Southwestern group on p.24. No Mahafaly-specific stress sentence exists in any opened source; Howe's own Mahafaly (Ejeda) word list (Table C.8) carries no stress marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog maha1309 'Mahafaly-Antanalana Malagasy' (dialects Mahafaly maha1311 and Antanalana/Tanalana anta1262, Ampanihy-Betioky-Onilahy region, SW Madagascar) has no ISO code and is subsumed under tdx 'Tandroy-Mahafaly Malagasy' (Glottolog tand1256), for which a separate audit folder exists (../tand1256/). The Howe 2017 statement quoted is pan-Malagasy with a sub-clause for 'western and southwestern dialects' (Dahl 1952); Howe's Southwestern group = Masikoro, Vezo, Mahafaly, Tandroy (p.24). Adelaar 2019's two stress-marked MHF forms are the only first-hand Mahafaly stress data opened.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Alexander. 2019. On the history of Malagasy terms for human body parts. In V. V. Sikorsky & V. A. Pogadaev (eds), Malay-Indonesian Studies XXI (Festschrift A. K. Ogloblin), 53-89. Moscow.
sources.note: Stress marked on every polysyllable (p.60 'Malagasy stress is contrastive'); only two Mahafaly (MHF) forms in the paper: 'TDR, VEZ, MHF tùmbukĕ' (antepenult before weak final -kĕ) and 'TDR, MHF, S-SKL rànju' (penult), pp.82-83; MHF source row not recoverable from the text layer of Table 2; no rule statement for Mahafaly.

sources.note: 'Mahafali' is among the dialects surveyed (habitat note, forms passim); Chap. VI 'L'accent tonique' pp.236-245 states for Malagasy as a whole that disyllabic roots are 'généralement paroxytons, très rarement oxytons', trisyllabic roots 'généralement proparoxytons, quelquefois paroxytons'; no dialect-specific remark (no mention of Mahafali/dialecte/Sakalava/Bara inside the chapter).

sources.note: The 'Sakalava' column is explicitly Mahafaly (p.VI 'le Sud ou Mahafaly'); the 'ACCENTUATION' section is only a typographic key (stressed syllable printed in italics, 'prononcée avec une pause et plus fortement que les autres'); italics are lost in the scanned; no rule of stress placement.
